name: Straw drinking for coffee
lead: Straw drinking for coffee is the habit of sipping coffee or other dark drinks through a straw so that less liquid touches the front teeth, in order to reduce visible staining. It is discussed in tooth-whitening and appearance communities as a low-effort preventive habit.

Dental references list frequent consumption of coffee, tea, red wine and cola as causes of extrinsic stain, linked to tannins and other pigments.[2][1] The same sources recommend identifying the cause of staining and note that most extrinsic stains are removed by cleaning.[2]
No studies of straw use and staining were found.
infobox: Reduce contact of coffee with front teeth

paras: Proponents use reusable or disposable straws with hot or iced coffee, arguing the drink bypasses the visible surfaces of the front teeth. How far liquid still contacts teeth during swallowing has not been measured in the sources reviewed.

Tannins in coffee and tea act as chromogens, and heavy consumption can stain enamel brown.[1] Extrinsic stains lie on the tooth surface; intrinsic stains form within it from causes such as ageing, trauma or fluorosis.[1] Treatment of extrinsic stain includes whitening toothpaste or professional scaling and polishing.[2] Staining is also affected by plaque and tobacco.[2]

card.summary: Sipping coffee through a straw to keep it off the front teeth; plausible to fans, but untested.
card.note: No studies of straw use and staining found.

quick.overview:
This habit means drinking coffee through a straw so less liquid reaches the visible surfaces of the teeth.

Dental sources say coffee and tea can cause extrinsic stain, but no study of straws was found.
quick.mechanism: The idea is reduced contact time between pigmented drink and front teeth.
quick.risks: No harms are documented; the effectiveness has not been measured.
